segments.text: Good morning everyone. In today's lecture we will be looking at the topic of meat production.
New research reveals that the environmental impact of beef is much more than that of other meat, including chicken or pork,
with one expert saying that eating less red meat would be a better way for people to cook carbon emissions than giving up their cars.
So, today we are going to look at why this might be.
First, I'll examine the impact of meat consumption on the environment.
Next, I'll discuss the issue of health.
Finally, I'll demonstrate how much meat is wasted in the production and consumption chain.
Firstly, we need to understand that meat is bad for you and bad for the environment.
At least that's the usual argument.
A study of tens of thousands of British people's daily eating habits shows that meat lovers'
diets cause double the climate warming emissions of vegetarian diets.
The fact is that livestock farming accounts for a huge 15% of all greenhouse gas emissions.
We can't all become vegetarian.
So just how much meat is it okay for an eco-citizen to eat?
It's not just pro-vegetarian demonstrators who are concerned about food's impact on
the climate. A major report concludes that food production is too close to the limits
of a safe operating space, defined by how much we need, how much we can produce, and
its impact on the climate. Meat is a major contributor to that. 80% of agricultural emissions
come from meat production, and the problem is getting worse. The heavy impact on the
environment of meat production was known, but the research shows a new scale and scope
of damage, particularly for beef. Production of this popular red meat requires 28 times
more land and 11 times more water than pork or chicken, and results in 5 times more climate
warming emissions. One compared to staples like potatoes, wheat and rice, the impact
of beef per calorie is even more extreme, requiring 160 times more land and producing
11 times more greenhouse gases. Agriculture is a significant driver of global warming
and causes 15% of all emissions, half of which are from livestock. Furthermore, the huge
amounts of grain and water needed to raise cattle are a concern for experts worried
about feeding an extra 2 billion people by 2050.
But previous calls for people to eat less meat in order to help the environment, or preserve
grain stocks, have been highly controversial.
Now, I'll turn to the issue of how much meat we consume.
As people get richer, the demand for protein gets stronger.
It's unrealistic to expect everyone to give up meat entirely, and many of the world's
poor need to increase their meat consumption to overcome malnutrition and food insecurity.
The solution is to eat less meat rather than no meat.
A study in 2007 estimated that the average person consumed 100 grams of meat a day or
about one burger, a quarter pounder is 113 grams.
The rich eat ten times more than the poor.
In other words, some people get ten burgers a day, while others get none.
The study showed that if every person in the world ate 50 grams of red meat and 40 grams
of white meat per day, by 2050 greenhouse gas emissions from meat production would stabilise
at 2005 levels, a target cited in national plans for agricultural emissions.
That's about one burger and one small chicken breast per person every two days.
So have a think about how much meat you eat each day.
Would you think about becoming a vegetarian?
So let's now consider how much meat is wasted.
The 2007 figures in the study didn't take into account the fact that we throw out a
lot of the animal mass produced, because we consider it inedible.
countries are the biggest offenders, whereas many other cultures are not put off by a meal
of brains or testicles. It is estimated that Americans and Australians throw out up to
half the cow mass they produce, and globally we discard between five and ten per cent of
the animal. This means we can only allow ourselves eighty to eighty-five grams of red
and white meat, or one burger and one chicken fillet every three days. Our allowance would
drop further if more people were as wasteful as the Americans and Australians. Also, according
to the research, one-third of all food produced is spoiled due to poor refrigeration, pests
and bulk packaging. All of this wastage encourages consumers to buy more than they can eat.
Okay, that's it for today. Any questions?
